visuals.title: What changed with each kind of support?
visuals.description: Comparison of the reported effort, difficulty and question-attempt results across two mathematics tasks. These are exploratory group comparisons, not scores of learning quality.
rows: AI tutor and search higher than human
visuals.caption: Later challenge choice showed no clear group difference. Table 2 reports adjusted comparisons; absence of a detected difference does not establish equivalence. This single-session study did not assess answer accuracy or lasting learning.

review.scope: Compared every displayed direction with Table 2 and retained exploratory, multiple-comparison and measurement limits. This is an AI-assisted check, not independent replication.

visuals.title: How many reasons made it into the recommendation?
visuals.description: Students researched sunscreen ingredients, then wrote advice from memory. Researchers counted how many of seven relevant points appeared in each response.
visuals.caption: Each bar shows a group average. The score counts reasons students gave for their advice on this one topic. It tells us little about how they would reason on a different topic.

review.scope: Checked the two group sizes, tool names, unadjusted means, seven-point maximum and writing task against the published PDF.

visuals.title: What score did students expect, and how did they do?
visuals.description: Students discussed a case in groups. Then each student predicted their score and took a four-question test on their own.
rows: Asked to work without AI (64 students)
visuals.caption: These are group averages. After accounting for class and discussion group, the study found a difference in test scores. The difference in predicted scores was inconclusive. Both groups took the test immediately after discussion.

review.scope: Checked both sets of reported means, group sizes, scoring range and timing against the publisher’s methods and Table 1. Checked the distinction between the two outcomes against Table 2.

visuals.title: Do hints help students learn more?
visuals.description: Stanford’s review describes three comparisons of AI tutoring. Students used different tools, in different settings.
rows: Students given an answer and explanation right away scored higher on a later test than those who got hints and encouragement first.
Students who practiced with a hint-based tutor scored higher on an exam than those who used a general-purpose chatbot.
The study found no clear improvement in what students knew when the chatbot added prompts about motivation or how to study.
visuals.caption: These are findings from separate studies, as reported by the review. The groups also differed in age, task and tool design. The comparisons leave open which features work best for a particular class.

source.locator: Key Findings on Students, “General-purpose AI vs. educational AI tools”; Appendix A

review.scope: Read the review’s comparison of Cao, Bastani and Fütterer and checked the setting, tool comparison and reported direction for each row. The three underlying studies were not independently reanalyzed.

visuals.title: What happened after students opened the practice exam?
visuals.description: Chatbot logs show how many practice sessions displayed a prompt and how many recorded a response.
visuals.caption: A student could open the exam several times. These counts describe sessions, and the answers were not a test of how much students learned.

review.scope: Checked the four counts against the Total column of the publisher’s Table 2 and checked the session definition in Practice intensity. Values are session counts, not percentages of individual students.

visuals.title: Who does the work when AI helps write a complaint?
visuals.description: Two perspectives from letters published in the Guardian.
rows: Long letters can make it harder to find the problem a tenant wants fixed.
Writing help may give someone a way to raise a grievance they struggled to put into words.
visuals.caption: These are individual perspectives. The letters give no count of how often either experience occurs.

review.scope: Checked speaker attribution and each position against the first and third letters. The two rows are paraphrased perspectives, not observations representative of all complaints.

visuals.title: What can a teacher see in a case assignment?
visuals.description: Two examples from Kearney’s proposed assessment framework.
headers: What the teacher still needs to know
rows: A student can keep a detailed record while accepting every suggestion. Which ideas did the student actually judge?
A student can weigh competing explanations and submit only a conclusion. Why did they choose it?
visuals.caption: Kearney proposes asking students to explain two decisions. These are imagined classroom cases. Their effect on learning has yet to be tested.

source.locator: Illustrative cases and worked example, pp. 8–10

review.scope: Compared both cases with the checked publisher-version notes and indexed primary PDF passages. Preserved the distinction between a hypothetical design and a tested classroom intervention.

visuals.title: Where did AI enter the writing process?
visuals.description: Colorado Public Radio interviewed two high school seniors and a university instructor about writing.
rows: She wrote her own literature essay, then gave AI her draft, the grading rubric and her teacher’s comments to get revision ideas.
He used AI to check punctuation and grammar in his college application essay.
He moved long writing assignments into class to watch students develop their work. That left less class time for other teaching.
visuals.caption: These are interview accounts of particular assignments. The reporting gives no comparison of how much students learned.

source.locator: Students and AI; Teachers and AI
source.attribution: Andrea Dukakis and Hayley Sanchez, CPR News (2026)

review.scope: Checked names, roles, actions and the time trade-off against the two sections in the original report.

visuals.title: What did 93 studies actually track?
visuals.description: Number of higher-education studies in Li and colleagues’ review that documented each kind of evidence.
rows: How students responded to AI output
Learning on a task without AI
Both the response to AI and learning without it
visuals.caption: A study can appear in several rows. In 22 of the 44 studies describing responses to AI, the evidence came from student reports or author statements.

source.locator: Results on processing evidence; Discussion, principal findings

review.scope: Verified the denominator, all four overlapping counts and the self-report qualification in the publisher’s results and discussion.

visuals.title: What kind of effort did students report?
visuals.description: Jia surveyed 1,050 university students about their experience with AI and their engagement in coursework.
rows: Operating the tool and checking its answers
Students reporting more of this effort tended to report lower engagement.
Working through ideas with AI feedback
Students reporting more of this effort tended to report higher engagement.
visuals.caption: Students answered the questions once. The survey cannot tell which experience came first or show how much anyone learned.

review.scope: Checked the definitions of the two measures, the signs in the regression model and the one-time survey design in the primary article.

visuals.title: Why did two estimates nearly cancel out?
visuals.description: Wang and colleagues combined data from 31 studies and estimated two links between AI use and critical thinking.
visuals.caption: These numbers describe the direction and strength of relationships in a statistical model. The interval for the combined link includes zero. Most studies measured people only once.

source.locator: Accepted manuscript, Figure 15 and accompanying results, pp. 19–20

review.scope: Checked each published standardized estimate and confidence interval against the accepted manuscript. The combined estimate is the value reported by the authors.

doi:10.1007/s42438-026-00721-w.reason: The proposed lab is a single worked example. The prose can explain why a student checks an assumption without turning an untested teaching idea into a sequence of measured steps.

doi:10.1007/s44163-026-02808-6.reason: The author compares two imagined disclosures and proposes a future test. A short example preserves the distinction between how readers might respond and what anyone observed.

url:https://www.edsurge.com/news/ai-has-.reason: The author tells how an abandoned vocabulary lesson informed one teacher’s classroom routine. Keeping the account in sequence preserves which lesson was imagined and which practices took place.

url:https://www.apa.org/pubs/reports/ai-.reason: The two objectives offer separate workplace recommendations. The examples and evidence limits fit in a short account; the report supplies no common measure for comparing their results.
